# Glossary ΓÇö plain English only

Every term used in this course, defined as if you've never seen Spark.
Updated as we learn. If a term is missing, ask and it gets added.

---

## The basics

| Term | Plain meaning | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Spark** | A program that processes data too big for one computer by splitting the work across several computers. | A catering company instead of one home cook. |
| **Data** | Information arranged in rows and columns ΓÇö like a spreadsheet. | A stack of order slips. |
| **Row** | One record. One order, one customer, one click. | One line in a spreadsheet. |
| **Column** | One field across all rows. | One column in a spreadsheet. |
| **DataFrame** | Spark's name for a table (rows + columns) that can be processed in parallel. | A spreadsheet you can hand to many workers at once. |
| **Schema** | The list of columns and their types (text, number, date). | The labels on a filing cabinet telling you what's inside. |

## The machines

| Term | Plain meaning | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Cluster** | A group of computers working together as one. | A restaurant with several kitchens. |
| **Node** | One computer inside a cluster. | One kitchen. |
| **Driver** | The program that runs *your* code. It decides what work to do and hands it out. It does **not** process the data. | Head chef: writes the plan and shouts orders. |
| **Executor** | A process on a worker machine that actually processes data and holds it in memory. | Line cook: does the actual cooking. |
| **Core** | One processor inside a machine. One core does one task at a time. | One stove. |
| **Cluster manager** | Software that hands out machines to Spark (YARN, Kubernetes, Standalone). | The landlord who assigns kitchens. |
| **Local mode (`local[*]`)** | Driver and executors all inside one program on your laptop. | A one-person kitchen doing every job. |
| **Serverless** | The platform starts and stops the machines for you; you never see them. | A takeaway service with invisible kitchens. |
| **Databricks** | A company that sells a managed Spark platform with extra tools. | A restaurant franchise: same cooking, nicer building. |

## The work

| Term | Plain meaning | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Job** | All the work triggered by **one action**. | One order from a customer. |
| **Stage** | A chunk of a job where no data has to be moved between machines. A job is cut into stages wherever a shuffle happens. | A cooking phase; after it, ingredients must be carried to another counter. |
| **Task** | The work of processing **one partition**. One task per partition. | One dish. |
| **Partition** | One chunk of the data. Data is always split into partitions. | One portion of ingredients. |
| **Transformation** | An instruction that describes a change (`select`, `filter`, `groupBy`). It does **nothing** on its own. | Writing a step in the recipe, not cooking it. |
| **Action** | An instruction that asks for a result (`show`, `count`, `write`). This is what starts the work. | Actually cooking and plating. |
| **Lazy evaluation** | Spark waits until an action before doing anything. Transformations only build a plan. | The chef reads the whole order before switching on the stove. |
| **Shuffle** | Moving data between machines so related rows end up together. Expensive. | Carrying ingredients from one kitchen to another. |
| **DAG** | The graph of steps Spark will perform, drawn from your transformations. | The recipe flowchart. |
| **Narrow dependency** | Each output partition needs only one input partition. No data movement. | One cook takes one tray and works on it. |
| **Wide dependency** | Output partitions need data from many input partitions ΓåÆ requires a shuffle. | Every cook needs something from every other tray. |
| **Stage boundary** | The point where a shuffle happens and a new stage begins. | The moment ingredients must be carried across the kitchen. |

## Performance words

| Term | Plain meaning | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Catalyst** | Spark's built-in planner that rewrites your query to run faster before executing it. | An experienced chef who rearranges your recipe to save time. |
| **Physical plan** | The concrete "how I will actually do it" that Spark prints with `explain()`. | The final kitchen work order. |
| **Predicate pushdown** | Reading only the rows that match your filter, instead of reading everything then filtering. | Skipping boxes whose label says "no 2024 data". |
| **Column pruning** | Reading only the columns you asked for. | Only opening the drawers you need. |
| **AQE (Adaptive Query Execution)** | Spark re-deciding some choices *while* the job runs, based on real data sizes. | The chef adjusting mid-service after seeing the actual portions. |
| **Photon** | Databricks' faster engine written in C++. Not part of open-source Spark. | A turbocharged stove only available in that franchise. |
| **Partial aggregation** | Counting/summing within each partition *before* moving data, so less data travels. | Each cook counts their own tray first, then reports one number. |
| **cache / persist** | Keep a result in memory so later steps don't recompute it. | Photocopying a document instead of walking back to the cabinet. |
| **Spill** | Running out of memory, so Spark writes data to disk temporarily. | The worktop is full, so items go on the floor. |
| **Evict** | Dropping cached data from memory because space ran out; it must be recomputed later. | Throwing a folder off the desk to make room. |
| **Lineage** | Spark's memory of *how* a DataFrame was built, allowing it to rebuild lost pieces. | The recipe lets you remake a dropped dish. |
| **Broadcast join** | Copying a small table to every machine so no data has to be shuffled. | Photocopying a small price list for every cook. |
| **Skew** | One partition holding far more data than the others, so one worker does most of the work. | One cook gets 90% of the orders. |

# Architecture I ΓÇö starting from zero

## The problem we're solving

You have **a table with 1 billion rows**. Your laptop has 16 GB of memory. It doesn't fit.

So you rent **3 computers** instead of 1. Now:

- The data gets **split** into 3 pieces, one per computer
- Each computer works on **its own piece**
- Someone has to **coordinate**: decide who does what, then collect the answers

That's the entire idea of Spark. Now the three roles.

## The 3 roles

| Role | Plain definition | Restaurant |
|---|---|---|
| **Driver** | The program running **your code**. It reads your instructions, makes a plan, and tells the workers what to do. **It does not process any data.** | Head chef: reads the order, writes the plan, shouts instructions |
| **Executor** | A process on a worker computer. It **holds data and does the actual processing**. | Line cook: chops, fries, plates |
| **Cluster manager** | Software that decides **which computers** Spark gets to use. | Landlord: assigns kitchens to the head chef |

Two facts to hold onto:

1. **The driver never touches the data.** It only plans and coordinates.
2. **Executors never plan.** They just do what they're told.

# Note 08 ΓÇö Architecture I: the cast

> Level: absolute beginner. Every term defined here.
> Status: **Part I complete.** Part II (job ΓåÆ stage ΓåÆ task, lineage) is next session.

---

## 1. The problem architecture solves

You have a table with **1 billion rows**. Your laptop has 16 GB of memory. It does not fit.

So you rent **3 computers**:

- The data is **split** into pieces, one per computer
- Each computer works on **its own piece**
- Something has to **coordinate**: decide who does what, then gather the answers

Spark is the software that does the splitting, the coordinating, and the gathering.

---

## 2. The three roles

| Role | Plain definition | Restaurant analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Driver** | The program that runs **your code**. It reads your instructions, builds a plan, and hands out work. **It never processes data.** | Head chef: reads the order, writes the plan, shouts instructions |
| **Executor** | A process on a worker computer. It **holds data in memory and does the actual processing**. | Line cook: chops, fries, plates |
| **Cluster manager** | Software that decides **which computers** Spark may use. Examples: Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes. | Landlord: assigns kitchens |

Two rules that explain almost every Spark behaviour:

1. **The driver never touches the data.** It only plans, schedules, and collects results.
2. **Executors never plan.** They do exactly what they are told.

---

## 3. The smaller pieces

| Term | Plain definition | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Cluster** | A group of computers working together as one system. | A restaurant with several kitchens |
| **Node** | One computer inside the cluster. | One kitchen |
| **Core** | One processor inside a machine. One core runs **one task at a time**. | One stove |
| **Task** | The work of processing **one partition**. | One dish |
| **Partition** | One chunk of the data. Data is always split into partitions. | One portion of ingredients |
| **Job** | All the work triggered by **one action** (`show`, `count`, `write`). | One customer order |
| **Stage** | A group of tasks with no data movement between them. A job is cut into stages at every shuffle. | A cooking phase |

---

## 4. The picture

```
   YOUR CODE  ("read the file, add up the amounts")
        Γöé
        Γû╝
   DRIVER  ΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇ builds the plan ΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓû║  "you 3, each take one piece"
        Γöé                                    Γöé
        Γöé                          ΓöîΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓö╝ΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÉ
        Γöé                          Γû╝         Γû╝         Γû╝
        Γöé                     EXECUTOR 1  EXECUTOR 2  EXECUTOR 3
        Γöé                     (piece 1)   (piece 2)   (piece 3)
        Γöé                          Γöé         Γöé         Γöé
        ΓööΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇ collects ΓùäΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓö┤ΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓö┤ΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÿ
                the answers
```

---

## 5. Where does the driver run? (deployment modes)

| Mode | Driver lives... | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **`local[*]`** | on your laptop, executors in the **same** process | learning, small data |
| **Standalone** | inside the cluster | simple clusters |
| **YARN** | on a cluster node | Hadoop shops |
| **Kubernetes** | in a pod | cloud-native |
| **Databricks serverless** | managed for you; executors are created per query and destroyed | your current setup |

**Why this matters:** `local[*]` is enough to learn, because the *cast is identical* ΓÇö it's just
all in one building.

**Databricks serverless specifics:** executors are ephemeral, `spark.sparkContext` and RDDs are
blocked, and the Storage tab may be unavailable. That is a platform restriction, not a Spark one.

---

## 6. Consequences you can already predict

| If you... | Then... | Why |
|---|---|---|
| call `collect()` on a huge DataFrame | driver may run out of memory | all rows are shipped to the driver |
| have 3 partitions on 8 cores | 5 cores idle | concurrency = `min(partitions, cores)` |
| call `show()` | a job starts | `show` is an action |
| call `filter()` | nothing happens | transformation, only extends the plan |

---

## 7. Check questions (still unanswered)

1. **Who holds the data while it's being processed ΓÇö the driver or the executors?**
2. **What is the driver's job, in your own words?**

---

## 8. Next: Architecture II
- How one action becomes **job ΓåÆ stages ΓåÆ tasks**
- **Narrow vs wide dependencies** (why shuffles create stage boundaries)
- **Lineage** and fault tolerance: what happens when an executor dies
- Hands-on: trace one query through every layer using `explain()`

2. **Work** on each chunk at the same time

| Job | What it means in plain words | Who it is |
|---|---|---|

   customer order  =  your code
   head chef       =  driver        (plans, shouts orders, never cooks)

```

**Rule 1:** the head chef doesn't cook.
**Rule 2:** the line cooks don't plan.

| Word | Plain meaning | Restaurant |
|---|---|---|
| **Partition** | one chunk of the data | one tray of ingredients |
| **Task** | the work of processing **one** partition | one dish |

[4 tasks]   [4 tasks]   [4 tasks]

| **Plan the work** | Reads *your* code, decides the steps, hands out jobs, collects the results | **Driver** |
| **Do the work** | Holds a chunk of data in memory and processes it | **Executor** |
| **Provide the computers** | Decides which machines Spark may use | **Cluster manager** |

### The restaurant picture

```
   customer order   =  your code
   head chef        =  driver          (plans, shouts orders, never cooks)
   line cooks       =  executors       (actually cook)
   landlord         =  cluster manager (gives you the kitchen)
```

**Rule 1:** the head chef does not cook.
**Rule 2:** the line cooks do not plan.

In Spark: **the driver never touches the data. The executors never decide anything.**

---

## 3. The work units

| Word | Plain meaning | Restaurant |
|---|---|---|
| **Partition** | one chunk of the data | one tray of ingredients |
| **Task** | the work of processing **one** partition | one dish |
| **Core** | one processor. It does **one task at a time** | one stove |

So the chain is always:

```
1 partition  ΓåÆ  1 task  ΓåÆ  1 core at a time
```

---

## 4. A concrete example

- 300 million rows
- 3 computers ├ù 4 cores each = **12 cores**
- Spark cuts the data into **12 partitions**

```
        DRIVER  "12 tasks, go"
              Γöé
   ΓöîΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓö╝ΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÇΓöÉ
   Γû╝          Γû╝          Γû╝
COMPUTER 1  COMPUTER 2  COMPUTER 3
4 cores     4 cores     4 cores
[4 tasks]   [4 tasks]   [4 tasks]
```

12 tasks, 12 cores ΓåÆ **all run at the same time. One round.**

Now change one number: only **3 partitions**.

```
3 tasks, 12 cores ΓåÆ 3 cores work, 9 cores sit idle
```

The job takes about **4 times longer** than it needed to. Nothing is broken ΓÇö it is just
wasting the computers you are paying for.

That single idea is called **parallelism**: how much work happens at the same time.

---

## 5. What happens when you run `df.show()`

Step by step:

1. **Driver** reads your code and builds a plan
2. **Driver** sends tasks to the executors
3. **Executors** process their partitions and send the answers back
4. **Driver** shows you the result

Every **action** (`show`, `count`, `write`) follows this path.

Every **transformation** (`filter`, `select`, `withColumn`) only edits the plan.
No data moves, no tasks run.

---

## 6. Two consequences you can now predict

| Situation | What happens | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `df.collect()` on 300M rows | the driver may run out of memory and crash | every row is shipped to the driver, which has limited memory |
| 3 partitions on 12 cores | 9 cores idle | concurrency = `min(partitions, cores)` |

---

## 7. Where does the driver live? (deployment modes)

| Mode | Driver lives... | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **`local[*]`** | on your laptop, executors in the **same** program | learning, small data |
| **Standalone** | inside the cluster | simple clusters |
| **YARN** | on a cluster node | Hadoop shops |
| **Kubernetes** | in a container pod | cloud-native setups |
| **Databricks serverless** | managed for you; executors are created per query and then destroyed | your current setup |

**Why this matters:** `local[*]` is enough to learn, because the cast is identical ΓÇö it is
just all inside one building.

**Databricks serverless specifics:** executors are temporary. `spark.sparkContext` and RDDs
are blocked, and the Storage tab may be missing. That is a *platform* rule, not a Spark rule.

---

## 8. Words used in this note

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Cluster** | a group of computers working as one system |
| **Node** | one computer inside the cluster |
| **Driver** | the program running your code; plans and coordinates |
| **Executor** | a process on a worker computer; holds data and does the work |
| **Cluster manager** | software that assigns machines (YARN, Kubernetes, Standalone) |
| **Partition** | one chunk of the data |
| **Task** | the work of processing one partition |
| **Core** | one processor; runs one task at a time |
| **Job** | all the work triggered by one action |
| **Action** | something that asks for a result (`show`, `count`, `write`) |
| **Transformation** | something that only describes a change (`filter`, `select`) |

---

## 9. Check questions (still open)

1. **Who actually processes the 300 million rows ΓÇö the driver or the executors?**
2. **What does the driver do all day?**

---

## 10. Next: Architecture II
- How one action becomes **job ΓåÆ stage ΓåÆ task**
- **Narrow vs wide dependencies** ΓÇö why a shuffle creates a new stage
- **Lineage** ΓÇö what happens when an executor dies mid-job
- Hands-on: trace one query through every layer using `explain()`

How will my data be used?

- V7 will not use and does not intend to use your data to fine-tune models.

Where is my data processed and stored?

Can the model providers that power Go train or tune their models using my data?

- No. V7 has an enterprise plan with all of the frontier model providers, this means none of your data can be used for training. The model providers themselves can retain any data sent to them for up to 30 days. This is the same for both Enterprise and Pro plans.

## [Processing regions | Help Center](https://help.intric.ai/en/docs/administration/governance/processing-regions/)

A security classification says how sensitive data is. Processing regions say where that data is allowed to be handled. They are two different questions, and a model has to satisfy both before Intric will offer it.

...

When it decides whether to offer you a model, Intric looks at where that modelΓÇÖs sub-processor is hosted and checks it against the regions the SpaceΓÇÖs classification permits. If the region isnΓÇÖt on the list, the model isnΓÇÖt available there ΓÇö regardless of how the model itself is classified.

...

Processing regions are configured per security classification, under Policies in Administration. You set them on the classification rather than on a Space, so every Space carrying that classification inherits the same restriction automatically ΓÇö and a Space admin canΓÇÖt loosen it.

Copilots and generative AI features aren't available in all regions and languages. - "command not found: subsub": open a new terminal window. If the problem continues, type the install command again.
- On Windows, PowerShell says "running scripts is disabled on this system": type `subsub.cmd` in place of `subsub` (for example `subsub.cmd doctor`), or type the install command again, which fixes it.
- The shortcut does nothing, or the page says "Open Sub-Sub with its shortcut": open Sub-Sub from the shortcut again (the page address changes each time Sub-Sub starts). If the problem continues, type `subsub web` in a terminal and read the message. The browser view writes a log to `~/.subsub/web.log`.
- The shortcut stopped working after an update or a move: type `subsub shortcut`.
- On Windows, the shortcut also opens a minimised window in the taskbar. That window is Sub-Sub itself: closing it stops Sub-Sub.
- The page says "Sub-Sub stopped": select Start again. If it stops again, type `subsub doctor`.
- Zotero asks for permission when Sub-Sub first changes something: select Always Allow.
- "This Go model requires Global regions": your OpenCode workspace allows only some regions. In OpenCode, open the workspace's Privacy settings and select Global, or choose another model.
- Sub-Sub says that web search is not set up: it still finds references in Crossref, Google Books, Internet Archive, Open Library and Wikidata. For web search, get a key at brave.com/search/api and type `subsub init`.
- "cannot use opencode-go/ΓÇª": you are not logged in to that provider, or the model name is wrong. Select the model button and save a key (in the terminal, `/login`), or change `models` in the settings file.
- `/profile` says "Sub-Sub no longer has profiles": every command is now in the Researcher. If you are in the Librarian, type `/researcher`. To read a paper with guidance, type `/read`. See Modes and commands.
- A command or a search tool is "part of the Researcher": type `/researcher`, or select Researcher at the top of the browser view.
- `/verify` says that reference checks need Starbuck: turn on "Reference checks (Starbuck)" in the panel on the left of the browser view, or type `subsub init --starbuck on`.
- Sub-Sub refuses a literature note: the note must say what Sub-Sub read (evidence: full text, abstract or metadata), and it can give page numbers only when it read the full text. A note written from the full text may quote only what the full text says: Sub-Sub compares each quote with the item's text in Zotero. Ask Sub-Sub to correct the note.
- A review note was "already applied": Sub-Sub does not apply a note twice. To apply it again, ask for it explicitly.
- Sub-Sub says that it does not draft text for assignments: this is on purpose. Use `/read` to read the papers with guidance, and `/lit reading list:` for a list of works to read. For a manuscript or a thesis, Sub-Sub drafts text when you ask.
- `/read` with the reason critique says that it read only the abstract: a critique needs the full text. Attach the PDF in Zotero, use Sub-Sub on your institution's network, or type `/request-copy` and the citekey.
- You deleted a conversation by mistake: Delete moves the file to `~/.subsub/trash`, in the same subfolder as before. Move it back to the same place in `~/.subsub/agent/sessions/`.

## [doomsday616/opencode-github-sync](https://github.com/doomsday616/opencode-github-sync)

You use OpenCode on more than one machine. Your config, agents, commands, skills
and MCP servers live on whichever one you touched last.

**opencode-github-sync** keeps them all in step through a private GitHub
repository ΓÇö as an OpenCode plugin, as a CLI, or both.

```bash
npm install -g opencode-github-sync
opencode-sync init          # creates the private repo and configures this machine
opencode-sync push

...

### Every other machine

```bash
opencode-sync link doomsday616/my-opencode-config
opencode-sync pull
```

Then restart OpenCode.

...

## Session sync

Off by default. Turn it on only for a private repository ΓÇö conversations are
private data.

```bash
opencode-sync sessions enable
opencode-sync sessions list
opencode-sync sessions include ses_065cad1caffeN3lf1RgLZno30   # pin one forever
opencode-sync sessions exclude ses_0ba19b4e7ffeMbSmWYi3Nj6xfZ  # never sync this one
```

### Why not just commit the database

A real OpenCode database reaches several gigabytes, almost all of it tool output
inside `part.data`. Git cannot delta-compress it, GitHub's LFS free tier is one
gigabyte, and copying a live database alongside its write-ahead log can capture
a torn state that only shows up much later.

So sessions are exported **one at a time**. Each becomes an independent gzipped
JSON shard holding its own rows plus the project and workspace rows it needs:

- **No large files.** Shards are small and compress well.
- **Conflicts isolate themselves.** Two machines working on different sessions
 touch different files, so git merges them with no special handling. The only
 real conflict is one session edited in two places, and there the newer
 `time_updated` wins ΓÇö an in-progress conversation is never clobbered by a
 stale copy.
- **You choose what travels.** A time window, an explicit include list, a
 project filter and a per-session size cap. Ancient sessions stay where they
 are.

Import is an upsert inside a transaction, so a failure leaves your database
exactly as it was.

## [neuronalism/opencode-session-manager-cli](https://github.com/neuronalism/opencode-session-manager-cli)

A simple CLI tool for managing OpenCode projects and sessions stored in SQLite. It can:
- handle renamed/removed project folders,
- batch export all sessions (with sub-sessions) of a project as markdown or raw JSON,
- import raw JSON sessions (with sub-sessions) into the database, and 
- sync project-stored JSON sessions with the local database, allowing cross-device project synchronization.

Tested on OpenCode v1.18.31 on Windows and Mac.

...

- Suppose you are working on a long conversation and want to *continue it on another machine*, but currently OpenCode does not support syncing conversations across multiple machines. The other machine will not have these conversations you had elsewhere. 
 - You can use this tool to export the raw conversation to the project folder, sync it, and then re-import it on the other machine. Your conversations (and the whole project!) will be fully preserved and you can continue working smoothly.
 - If you are working on both Windows and Mac machines, re-importing the conversations handles path issues smoothly, as all files are treated relative to the project root.
- Suppose you moved your project folder to another location (or just renamed it for any reason), but OpenCode still has the old path in the database and won't recognize your new location. 
 - You can use this tool to update the path in the OpenCode database and have all your conversations back.
 - You can even *merge* multiple projects into one by "moving" the old project to the new path. Then you will see all your conversations in the merged project.
 - The old project paths don't even have to exist when moving, since this is only manipulating the OpenCode database; you need to manually move any other files in the project.

...

- **Full conversation trees.** OpenCode's `export` only emits the one session you name (as of version 1.17.8). Its subagent sessions are **not** exported ΓÇö their IDs only appear as strings inside a parent's tool-call metadata. Re-importing such an export therefore **loses every subagent session permanently**. This tool exports and imports the **entire tree** (root + all descendants), so a multi-agent conversation round-trips intact.
- **Batch operations.** `export project` / `import project` work on every session of a project at once, instead of one session at a time.
- **Two-way sync.** `sync project` reconciles the database and the project folder in both directions (new / updated / deleted), with conflict resolution and deletion propagation ΓÇö none of which the built-in commands offer.
- **Cross-machine path handling.** Imported sessions get their absolute paths rewritten to the local project directory (handling Windows Γåö Mac differences automatically); the built-in import keeps the exporting machine's paths.
- **No runtime dependency.** This tool talks to the SQLite database directly (`--db `), so it works even when the `opencode` CLI itself can't run, and can target any database file.
- **Safe writes.** Every database mutation goes through a WAL checkpoint + timestamped backup + single transaction with rollback.

...

#### Syncing

`sync project` reconciles a project's conversations **both ways** between the OpenCode database and the project's `.opencode/raw_conversations/` folder. Once that folder is kept in sync across machines (git, cloud drive, ΓÇª), running `sync` on each machine keeps the local DB consistent with it in **both** directions ΓÇö no manual export/import round-trip.

The simplest way to keep a project portable:

```
# on machine A
ocsm sync project --from /path/to/proj      # writes DB sessions into the folder
# git push / cloud-sync the project folder
# on machine B (after git pull)
ocsm sync project --from /path/to/proj      # pulls new folder sessions into the local DB
```

...

- **Identity & freshness**: sessions are matched by `id`; which copy is newer is decided by

...

- **Classification**:

...

- on both sides, same `time_updated` ΓåÆ no-op;
 - on both sides, different `time_updated` ΓåÆ **conflict**;

...

- **Conflicts** are resolved by `--on-conflict`:
 - `ask` (default): per-session prompt ΓÇö *keep DB / keep folder / skip* ΓÇö like a file-copy dialog. Needs a TTY; in a non-interactive shell it aborts with an error rather than silently overwriting (use `newer`/`skip` to run unattended).
 - `newer`: the copy with the larger `time_updated` wins (tie ΓåÆ skip).
 - `skip`: leave both copies untouched.
- **Deletion propagation**: if a session the manifest remembers later vanishes from one side, `sync` removes it from the other. **The first sync (no manifest) never deletes** ΓÇö every session is treated as new; deleting the manifest resets to that safe behavior. Deletions are whole-tree (removing a root session removes its subagents) and are confirmed interactively (default `N`) unless `-y` is given.
- **Safety**: DB writes reuse the same pipeline as `import` ΓÇö WAL checkpoint + timestamped `.bak` backup + single transaction with rollback. Updating an existing session is done as DELETE + INSERT (its messages/parts may have changed). Imported `project_id` is stamped with the registered project covering the target directory (nearest `project.worktree` / `project_directory` root), falling back to `global` only for unregistered directories.
- **No content merge**: a session is always taken wholesale from one side ΓÇö `sync` never merges messages field-by-field.

## [Sync OpenCode Sessions Across Devices | Reinstate](https://reinstate.dev/integrations/opencode)

# Sync OpenCode Sessions Across Devices | Reinstate

> Reinstate encrypts and syncs OpenCode sessions across devices, natively resumes and forks them, and hands off into or out of OpenCode as a structured checkpoint.

OpenCode reaches T5 in stable v0.6.0: encrypted same-vendor session sync, on top of T3 native resume and fork, T4 structured handoff destination, and T2 handoff source. Certified by native Windows x64 tagged-artifact acceptance PASS under the single-platform waiver in ADR 0005; Apple Silicon macOS acceptance is deferred to #403. Reinstate extracts a portable document from OpenCode's embedded SQLite store and reassembles it in the destination's own store. OpenCode-to-OpenCode sync only.

...

## How OpenCode session sync works

OpenCode keeps every session in one embedded SQLite database rather than one file per session, so the synced unit is a portable, deterministic JSON document extracted from the`session`, `project`, `message`, and `part` tables, with every absolute path normalized to a `$${HOME}` /`$${REPO:}` token. The `credential`, `account`,`control_account`, and `account_state` tables are never opened.

1. Export reads the session's rows through the embedded store, tokenizes every known path, and writes a single portable document as one tar entry.
2. Restore writes that document back into the destination's own `opencode.db` through a checkpointed working copy, fingerprint-guarded and backed up, then an atomic rename so a concurrent vendor write cannot corrupt the store.
3. Native resume and fork call OpenCode's own continuation flags ΓÇö`opencode --session ` and `opencode --session --fork`ΓÇö against the restored session, since OpenCode has no separate `resume` or`fork` verb.
4. A handoff into or out of OpenCode starts a new session through a bounded bootstrap and a private, inspectable projection; it is never a cross-agent resume.

...

Reinstate reads the local OpenCode store and does not call a hosted OpenCode API or require OpenCode account credentials. The `credential`, `account`,`control_account`, and `account_state` tables are excluded from every export, and a round-trip test fails if a credential value appears in one. Storage credentials stay in the operating system keyring.

## [ErcinDedeoglu/opencode-sync](https://github.com/ErcinDedeoglu/opencode-sync)

# OpenCode Sync

Sync your OpenCode configuration, sessions, and data across multiple machines using a private GitHub repository.

## Features

- **Sync Everything** - Config, sessions, messages, credentials, prompts, and more
- **Multi-Machine Support** - Safely sync across laptops, VMs, and servers simultaneously
- **Conflict Resolution** - Vector clocks detect conflicts, three-way merge resolves them
- **Encrypted Credentials** - AES-256-GCM encryption for sensitive data
- **Auto-Sync** - Syncs on startup, on file changes (5s debounce, 30s max), and every 5 minutes
- **Offline-Friendly** - Works offline, syncs when reconnected
- **Atomic Updates** - Uses Git's compare-and-swap for safe concurrent access

## Installation

**Step 1:** Install the package in your OpenCode config directory:

```bash
# Linux/macOS
cd ~/.config/opencode && npm install oc-sync

# Windows (PowerShell)
cd $HOME\.config\opencode; npm install oc-sync
```

**Step 2:** Register the plugin in `opencode.json` (in config directory):

```json
{
  "plugin": ["oc-sync"]
}
```

...

## What Gets Synced

| Category | Data | Default |
|----------|------|---------|
| Config | `opencode.json`, agents, commands, modes, tools, themes | Γ£à Enabled |
| State | Model selections, prompt history, stashed prompts | Γ£à Enabled |
| Credentials | OAuth tokens, MCP auth (encrypted) | Γ£à Enabled |
| Sessions | Session metadata and history | Γ£à Enabled |
| Messages | Conversation messages and parts | Γ£à Enabled |
| Projects | Project configurations | Γ£à Enabled |
| Todos | Task lists and session diffs | Γ£à Enabled |

...

### Vector Clocks for Conflict Detection

Each machine maintains a logical timestamp. When syncing:

1. **Equal** - Both in sync, no action needed
2. **Local Ahead** - Safe to push
3. **Remote Ahead** - Need to pull
4. **Concurrent** - Both changed, needs merge

### Three-Way Merge

When conflicts occur:

1. Find common ancestor (last synced version)
2. Compute diffs from ancestor to local and remote
3. If diffs don't overlap -> auto-merge
4. If diffs overlap -> apply conflict strategy

### What is implemented

- Configuration, skills, plugins and machine-local overrides via a private GitHub repository.
- Selected conversations as compressed JSON shards, never a live SQLite database in Git.
- Non-destructive SQLite UPSERT and preservation of existing project metadata, including `global`.
- Deterministic serialization with canonical ordering; unchanged exports stay byte-identical.
- Whole-batch transactional session import, schema/ownership validation and integrity checks before commit.
- Verified SQLite snapshots before modifying session data, with configurable backup retention.
- Per-session content baselines to detect divergent edits, including message changes without a timestamp change.
- Canonical-to-local path mappings, reversed on export.
- `doctor`, `backup`, offline `restore`, and isolated `--dry-run` previews.
- A local process lock and debounced auto-push. This is not a distributed multi-writer lock.

...

### First device

```sh
gh auth login
omds init my-opencode-config
omds sessions enable
omds doctor
omds push --dry-run
omds push

```

Start OpenCode once before importing conversations so it creates its own database schema and synthetic project. Configuration and session settings are stored in `~/.config/opencode/opencode-sync.jsonc`; the legacy filename is kept for migration compatibility.

### Second device

```sh
gh auth login
omds link YOUR_ACCOUNT/my-opencode-config
omds sessions enable
omds pull --dry-run
omds pull

```

Use a different `machineAlias` on each device. Keep credentials local and review machine-specific paths before starting OpenCode. See `examples/work-laptop.jsonc` and `examples/home-laptop.jsonc`.

...

`autoPullOnStartup` checks for incoming changes at startup. `autoPushOnIdle` is opt-in and waits for a successful initial pull; errors are logged and surfaced as notifications. Restart OpenCode after changes to imported configuration or sessions. Wait for a successful push before switching computers; closing the app or losing the network can interrupt a sync.

### Session visibility in Desktop

OpenCode Desktop scopes the visible chat list to the currently opened project directory. A successful import can therefore leave chats hidden when Desktop is still opened in another directory. `omds sessions locations` lists root/child sessions by directory, and `omds doctor` compares them with the Desktop `lastProject` state when that state can be read. The check is diagnostic only: OMDS does not rewrite OpenCode Desktop UI state automatically. Open the reported directory in Desktop to see those chats.

...

### Limitations you must understand

A sync transfers history and configuration, not the project's source files, browser profiles, active processes, external tool-output files or API credentials. Transfer project files separately. Path mapping covers session `directory`/`path` and project `worktree`, not every path embedded in message text or tool JSON.

Time/count/size limits select what gets exported. Existing remote shards are not automatically deleted when one device lacks a session or its selection window expires. Git history may retain data even after a file is removed.

A private repository is access control, not end-to-end encryption. Conversations can contain secrets even when credential-file sync is disabled. The credential scanner is a best-effort guard, not proof that a repository is free of secrets.

Conflicting sessions stop the import for manual review. There is no automatic merge of competing conversations. `--dry-run` uses a disposable snapshot and can require additional disk space; previews with `extraPaths` are refused. Local locking does not prevent simultaneous writers on other computers.

## [OpenCode session sync ΓÇö continue on any device ┬╖ Agent Context Sync](https://www.agentctxsync.com/en/agents/opencode/)

OpenCode's CLI and desktop builds share a single database, which makes it the least fussy agent to sync: whatever you wrote through either entry point comes along in one go.

## Where OpenCode keeps its sessions

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Database | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/opencode.db` (SQLite) |
| Tables | `session` / `message` / `part` |
| Shared by | CLI and desktop 1.x use the same store and the same tables |

If you have moved `XDG_DATA_HOME`, the adapter follows it.

## Connecting it

1. Open the setup help page, pick OpenCode, and download the client package (server address pre-filled).
2. On first run, execute `install-deps.bat` (Windows) or `./install-deps.sh` (macOS / Linux).
3. Register with the generated command ΓÇö your workspace API key is already filled in. The client starts as `HERMES_SYNC_AGENT=opencode`.
4. Restart OpenCode.

First start pulls incrementally; an empty server gets a full push to complete the pairing; then it syncs every 5 minutes.

## Behaviour worth knowing

- Written in the desktop row shape ΓÇö session ids carry the `ses_` prefix (`msg_` for messages, `prt_` for parts), timestamps are milliseconds and the `model` column is written as `{id, providerID}` JSON. A synced session therefore looks exactly like a local one and opens normally.
- Foreign sessions get normalised ΓÇö a session arriving from another agent gets a `ses_` id through the id mapper and round-trips with stable dedupe, so repeated syncs do not pile up duplicates.
- Projects resolve from the directory ΓÇö `project_id` is derived from where the session lives, so project cards line up.
- Database writes only ΓÇö your files are not rewritten, and an interrupted sync cannot leave a corrupt store behind.

## Across devices, across agents

Install the OpenCode client on two machines, connect both to the same workspace, and a day looks like this: at work you have the CLI agent refactor a module, at home you open the same session in the desktop app and ask why the refactor left that one branch alone. Handing it to Hermes or Oh My Pi works too ΓÇö same pool.

Now I have enough. Two answers:

1. **Live sync**: OpenCode has no built-in cloud sync. Sessions live in a local SQLite DB. Options:
   - Community plugins: `opencode-sync` (ErcinDedeoglu) with auto-sync every 5 min via private GitHub repo; `opencode-github-sync`; `opencode-multidevice-sync`.

# Part 1 ΓÇö Setting up Machine B

Machine B needs **4 tools** + **5 commands**.

## Prerequisites

| Tool | Why | Install |
|---|---|---|
| **Git** | the sync uses git | `winget install --id Git.Git -e` |
| **Node.js 22+** | runs the sync plugin | `winget install --id OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS -e` |
| **GitHub CLI** | authenticates the private repo | `winget install --id GitHub.cli -e` |
| **OpenCode desktop** | the app itself | https://opencode.ai (sign in) |

> ΓÜá∩╕Å Install these **before** opening OpenCode, then **restart your terminal** so PATH updates.

## The 5 commands (in order)

```powershell
# 1. install the sync plugin
npm install -g opencode-github-sync

# 2. sign in to GitHub (one-time, opens browser)
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web

# 3. point at the private sync repo
opencode-sync link bsocialg-cmd/opencode-sync-private

# 4. pull the shared config (first sync: keeps the repo's version)
opencode-sync pull

# 5. turn on the every-5-minutes job
opencode-sync autosync install
opencode-sync autosync enable
```

## Then get the course files

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/bsocialg-cmd/sppark-learn
```

Open **that folder** in OpenCode (not some other folder) ΓÇö the desktop app only shows chats for the open directory.

## Optional: load a past conversation

```powershell
opencode session import sessions/exports/2026-10-31-spark-course.json
```

Read-only in practice ΓÇö continuing it there starts a separate branch of the conversation, it doesn't share state.

## Do **not** do this on B

```powershell
opencode-sync sessions enable   # Γ¥î broken on OpenCode 2.x
```

## Verify it worked

```powershell
opencode-sync status      # should show the repo + machine name
opencode-sync pull        # should say "already up to date"
```

---

# Part 2 ΓÇö How Windows runs it every 5 minutes

`opencode-sync autosync install` registers a **Windows Task Scheduler** task. I inspected yours ΓÇö this is exactly what exists:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Task name** | `opencode-github-sync` |
| **Location** | `\` (Task Scheduler Library root) |
| **Runs as** | `TahilMirza`, limited privileges (no admin) |
| **Action** | `conhost.exe --headless node ...\opencode-github-sync\dist\cli\index.js autosync run` |
| **Trigger 1** | **every 5 minutes** (`PT5M`), starting 21:32 |
| **Trigger 2** | **at logon** |
| **Trigger 3/4** | **on session unlock / connect** (resume from sleep) |
| **Overlap rule** | `IgnoreNew` ΓÇö if a run is still going, the next is skipped |
| **Missed runs** | `StartWhenAvailable` ΓÇö catches up after sleep/offline |
| **Last result** | `0` = success ┬╖ **next run 21:42** |

So it's not a background service ΓÇö it's a **scheduled task fired by Windows**, roughly:

```
logon         ΓåÆ run
unlock/sleep  ΓåÆ run
every 5 min   ΓåÆ run
```

## See it yourself

**GUI:**
```
Win + R ΓåÆ taskschd.msc ΓåÆ Task Scheduler Library ΓåÆ opencode-github-sync
```
The **Triggers** tab shows the 5-minute repetition; **History** shows every run and result.

**PowerShell:**
```powershell
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "opencode-github-sync" | Select-Object TaskName, State
Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName "opencode-github-sync"   # last run, result, next run
```

## Control it

```powershell
opencode-sync autosync status     # is it on, last error
opencode-sync autosync run        # run one pass right now
opencode-sync autosync pause 4    # pause for 4 hours
opencode-sync autosync disable    # keep the task, stop it running
opencode-sync autosync uninstall  # remove the scheduled task entirely
```

## Changing the interval

The plugin hardcodes 5 minutes, but the trigger is a normal Windows task:
`taskschd.msc` ΓåÆ double-click the task ΓåÆ **Triggers** tab ΓåÆ Edit ΓåÆ *Repeat task every* ΓåÆ change to 15 minutes / 1 hour. Windows uses the task, not the plugin, so your change sticks.

2. **Pull before you edit** on the second machine. If you forget, git will refuse the push (`non-fast-forward`) ΓÇö nothing breaks, you just pull and retry.
3. **Config conflicts:** the plugin decides per file (`--prefer repo|local`, `--force`). If you change a setting on both machines, the newer sync wins and the other change is lost.
4. **Chats still don't sync** ΓÇö that limitation doesn't change with direction. Only files and config.

## Setup detail for PC B (easy to miss)

Git needs an identity before it can commit:

```powershell
git config --global user.name  "bsocialg-cmd"
git config --global user.email "bsocialg-cmd@users.noreply.github.com"
```

Without that, the **plugin's commits fail** and the course repo `git commit` fails too.

## What happens when a conflict occurs

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| B edited a file A didn't touch | merges cleanly Γ£à |
| Both edited the same file | `git pull` reports a conflict ΓåÆ pick one version |
| Plugin sees two config versions | newer wins, other is overwritten ΓÜá∩╕Å |

Nothing gets silently corrupted ΓÇö git is conservative. Worst case you choose which version to keep.

## My side, automatically

From now on, at the start of each session I'll run:

```
git pull --rebase
```

so if you worked on PC B, your commits land here before I edit anything. That's the one habit that prevents 90% of these problems.

---

Short version: **yes, B can push, and A will pick it up.** Just always pull before editing, and never run two machines on the same file at the same time.

# Lesson 2 ΓÇö How Spark Works: Architecture

**Level:** complete beginner ┬╖ **Time:** 45ΓÇô60 min ┬╖ **Prerequisites:** none

## What you will be able to do

By the end of this lesson you can:
1. Explain what a **driver**, an **executor** and a **cluster manager** do.
2. Explain what a **partition**, a **task** and a **core** are, and how they relate.
3. Predict how long a job takes from the number of partitions and cores.
4. Trace what happens, step by step, when you call `df.show()`.

---

## Words you will meet (nothing assumed)

| Word | Meaning, in one line |
|---|---|
| **Data** | Information in rows and columns ΓÇö like a spreadsheet |
| **Cluster** | A group of computers working together as one system |
| **Node** | One computer inside a cluster |
| **Driver** | The program that runs *your* code and plans the work |
| **Executor** | A program on a worker computer that does the actual processing |
| **Cluster manager** | Software that decides which computers Spark may use |
| **Partition** | One chunk of the data |
| **Task** | The work of processing one partition |
| **Core** | One processor; it runs one task at a time |
| **Action** | Something that asks for a result: `show`, `count`, `write` |
| **Transformation** | Something that only describes a change: `filter`, `select` |

---

## Part 1 ΓÇö The problem

You have a spreadsheet with **300 million rows** of sales data.

Your laptop has 16 GB of memory. The file does not fit. You cannot even open it.

You have two choices:

1. **Buy a bigger computer.** Expensive, and one day the data gets bigger again.
2. **Use several ordinary computers at once.** Cheap, and it scales forever.

Spark chooses option 2. And that choice creates three jobs that must be done:

- **Cut** the data into manageable chunks
- **Work** on the chunks at the same time
- **Gather** the results back together

Everything in this lesson is about *who does those three jobs*.

---

## Part 2 ΓÇö The three jobs (and the people who do them)

| Job | Who does it | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Plan and coordinate | **Driver** | Reads your code, builds a plan, hands out work, collects results |
| Do the actual work | **Executor** | Holds a chunk of data in memory and processes it |
| Supply the computers | **Cluster manager** | Decides which machines Spark gets to use |

### The restaurant picture ≡ƒì╜∩╕Å

```
   the customer's order   =   your code
   the head chef          =   driver           (plans, shouts orders, never cooks)
   the line cooks         =   executors        (chop, fry, plate)
   the landlord           =   cluster manager  (gives you the kitchen)
```

Two rules follow, and they explain almost everything later in the course:

> **Rule 1 ΓÇö The head chef does not cook.**
> The driver never processes the data.
>
> **Rule 2 ΓÇö The line cooks do not plan.**
> Executors never decide anything. They do exactly what they are told.

### Why this matters

When something is slow, the first question is always: *is the driver the bottleneck, or the executors?*
- Driver bottleneck ΓåÆ you asked it to hold data (e.g. `collect()`)
- Executor bottleneck ΓåÆ too few partitions, or too little memory

---

## Part 3 ΓÇö The work units

Spark cannot give "300 million rows" to one worker. It **cuts the data into partitions**.

| Word | Meaning | Restaurant |
|---|---|---|
| **Partition** | one chunk of the data | one tray of ingredients |
| **Task** | the work of processing one partition | one dish |
| **Core** | one processor; does one task at a time | one stove |

The chain is always the same:

```
one partition  ΓåÆ  one task  ΓåÆ  one core at a time
```

**The relay-race picture ≡ƒÅâ**
Twelve runners (cores), twelve batons (tasks). Everyone runs at once and the race finishes in
one round. But if you only have three batons (three partitions), nine runners stand and watch.

### The one formula to remember

```
tasks running at the same time  =  min( partitions , cores )
```

- **Too few partitions** ΓåÆ some cores sit idle. You are paying for computers that do nothing.
- **Too many partitions** ΓåÆ each task is tiny, and the fixed cost of starting a task is bigger
  than the work itself.

Think of it as: *enough trays for every stove, but not so many that the cook spends all day
walking back and forth.*

---

## Part 4 ΓÇö One action, step by step

You type:

```python
df.show()
```

What actually happens:

```
1. DRIVER reads your code
        Γöé
2. DRIVER builds a plan ("read the file, filter, group, show")
        Γöé
3. DRIVER splits the plan into stages and tasks
        Γöé
4. DRIVER sends tasks to the EXECUTORS
        Γöé
5. EXECUTORS read their partitions, do the work, send answers back
        Γöé
6. DRIVER collects the answers and shows them to you
```

Now compare with a transformation:

```python
df.filter(F.col("amount") > 100)
```

Nothing on that list happens. Not one step. The driver only writes down an instruction for later.
The work starts at **step 1** only when an action arrives.

> **Action = start the engine. Transformation = add a note to the plan.**

---

## Part 5 ΓÇö Where does the driver live?

| Mode | Driver livesΓÇª | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `local[*]` | on your laptop, executors in the same program | learning, small data |
| **Standalone** | inside the cluster | simple clusters |
| **YARN** | on a cluster node | Hadoop shops |
| **Kubernetes** | in a container pod | cloud-native setups |
| **Databricks serverless** | managed for you; executors are created and destroyed per query | your setup |

`local[*]` is enough to learn, because the cast is identical ΓÇö the whole restaurant is just
inside one building.

In your Databricks sandbox: the driver is managed, executors are temporary, and some commands
(`df.rdd`, `spark.sparkContext`) are blocked. That is a **platform** rule, not a Spark rule.

---

## Part 6 ΓÇö What architecture lets you predict

| If youΓÇª | ThenΓÇª | Because |
|---|---|---|
| call `collect()` on 300M rows | the driver may crash | every row is shipped to the driver |
| have 3 partitions on 12 cores | 9 cores idle, ~4x slower | `min(3, 12) = 3` |
| call `show()` | a job starts | it is an action |
| call `filter()` | nothing happens | it is a transformation |
| lose one executor mid-job | the job continues | tasks are recomputed on another executor |

---

## Part 7 ΓÇö Exercises (do these, don't just read)

**Exercise 1 ΓÇö draw it**
Draw your own Databricks setup: one driver box, one executor box, and label the parts.
Put the words *driver, executor, core, task, partition* on the drawing.

**Exercise 2 ΓÇö the maths**
A job has **20 partitions** and the cluster has **8 cores**.
1. How many tasks are created?
2. How many run at the same time?
3. How many rounds ("waves")?
4. Roughly how much faster would it be with 4 partitions instead of 20? *(careful ΓÇö think)*

**Exercise 3 ΓÇö who does what**
For each, say whether it is **driver work** or **executor work**:
- reading a Parquet file
- deciding how many tasks to create
- summing numbers inside one partition
- printing the result to your screen

**Exercise 4 ΓÇö read a real plan**
In Databricks run:
```python
spark.range(1000).groupBy((F.col("id") % 10).alias("g")).count().explain()
```
Find `splits=`. What does the number mean? Can you find the word `Exchange`?

---

## Part 8 ΓÇö Checkpoint (answer out loud, in your own words)

1. Who processes the data ΓÇö driver or executors?
2. What does the driver do all day?
3. What is a partition, and why does the number matter?
4. 6 partitions on 12 cores ΓÇö is anything wasted?
5. Which one starts the work: `filter` or `count`?

---

## Part 9 ΓÇö Summary card

```
DRIVER      plans, schedules, collects      (never touches data)
EXECUTORS   hold partitions, do the work    (never plan)
CLUSTER MGR gives out the machines

partition ΓåÆ task ΓåÆ one core at a time
concurrency = min(partitions, cores)

action        ΓåÆ starts a job
transformation ΓåÆ only edits the plan
```

**Next lesson:** how one action becomes **jobs ΓåÆ stages ΓåÆ tasks**, and why a shuffle splits a job
into stages (Architecture II).

| Mode | Driver | Used for |

| `local[*]` | your laptop, executors in the same program | learning |
| Standalone | inside the cluster | simple clusters |
| YARN | a cluster node | Hadoop shops |
| Kubernetes | a container | cloud setups |
| Databricks serverless | managed for you | your sandbox |

`local[*]` is enough to learn ΓÇö the same restaurant, just one building.

In your Databricks sandbox, `df.rdd` and `spark.sparkContext` are blocked. That's a **platform** rule, not a Spark rule.

---

## Part 6 ΓÇö What you can now predict

| If youΓÇª | ThenΓÇª | Because |
|---|---|---|
| `collect()` 300M rows | the driver may crash | every row is shipped to it |
| 3 partitions on 12 cores | 9 idle, ~4x slower | `min(3,12)=3` |
| call `show()` | a job starts | it's an action |
| call `filter()` | nothing happens | it's a transformation |
| lose an executor | the job continues | tasks get recomputed elsewhere |

---

## Exercises (do them, don't just read)

1. **Draw it.** One driver box, one executor box. Label: driver, executor, core, task, partition.
2. **The maths.** 20 partitions, 8 cores ΓåÆ how many tasks? how many run at once? how many rounds? Would 4 partitions be 5x faster? *(careful)*
3. **Who does what?** driver or executor: reading a Parquet file ┬╖ choosing task count ┬╖ summing within a partition ┬╖ printing to your screen.
4. **Read a plan.** Run `spark.range(1000).groupBy((F.col("id") % 10).alias("g")).count().explain()` and find `splits=`.

---

## Checkpoint ΓÇö answer in your own words

1. Who processes the data: driver or executors?
2. What does the driver do all day?
3. What is a partition, and why does the number matter?
4. 6 partitions on 12 cores ΓÇö what's wasted?
5. Which starts the work: `filter` or `count`?
